The heating contrast is continental, the wind reversal involves the whole lower atmosphere, and the onset can be startlingly abrupt — the flow flips and the rains arrive within days, after weeks of building heat and humidity that locals experience as an unbearable held breath. Agriculture, reservoirs, and entire economies are scheduled to the flip. A rainy season is weather that happens to be wet; a monsoon is the atmosphere changing its circulation, wholesale, twice a year, because a continent and an ocean cannot agree on a temperature.
I read that a hurricane's low pressure literally lets the sea rise up under the storm. How big is that effect by itself?

It is real, it has a name — the inverted barometer effect — and its exchange rate is easy to remember: for every hectopascal the air pressure drops, the sea surface beneath rises about one centimeter, because the reduced weight of air lets the water surface bulge up until the pressures balance at depth. Take a storm whose center is 60 hectopascals below the surrounding pressure:

About 60 centimeters of rise from the pressure effect alone. Honest accounting, though: that is the smaller part of storm surge. The larger part is mechanical — the storm's winds dragging across hundreds of kilometers of shallow coastal water and physically piling it against the shore, which in the great historical surges has contributed several meters, arriving on top of the tide. The pressure bulge matters because it is part of the total and because it is so counterintuitive: a meter-scale ocean response to nothing but the weight of air. It also runs in reverse under strong highs, pressing the sea surface down by the same exchange rate. The ocean's surface is, among other things, a barometer with a very slow, very large dial.
It's 20 degrees at the trailhead. The summit is 3 kilometers up. Roughly how cold should I dress for, if it's a normal day?

On a normal day the atmosphere's temperature falls with height at the environmental lapse rate, about 6.5 °C per kilometer — 'normal' here meaning the long-run average arrangement, not a law. Over 3 kilometers:
A drop of 19.5 degrees, so:

About 0.5 °C at the summit — dress for a twenty-degree colder world: freezing level, real layers, wind shell. Two honest caveats. First, the actual lapse rate on the day is whatever the day's air mass says: in a dry, unstable afternoon it can approach the parcel rate of 9.8 °C/km (a summit near −9 °C), while under an inversion the summit can be warmer than the valley, which is why the rule fails gloriously on some still winter mornings. Second, wind and sun exposure at a summit amplify whatever the thermometer says. But as a planning number, 6.5 per kilometer has saved more hikers from misery than any other single figure in mountain weather.
On winter nights the valley fills with fog and pollution while the hillsides above are clear. What traps everything down there?

A temperature inversion — the atmosphere's layering turned upside down. Normally temperature falls with height; in an inversion, a layer of warm air sits on top of colder surface air like a lid on a pot. The cold surface layer forms on clear, calm nights as the ground radiates heat away and chills the air it touches (and in valleys, cold air draining off the slopes deepens the pool). The warm layer above may be air that subsided from a high-pressure system or simply yesterday's milder air that the night's shallow cooling never reached.

The trap is about buoyancy. Pollution, fog droplets, smoke, and cold itself all stay in the surface layer because that air is denser than the air above it — a parcel nudged upward enters warmer, lighter surroundings and sinks back. Vertical mixing, the atmosphere's normal housekeeping, switches off. Everything emitted into the pool — exhaust, wood smoke, condensed vapor — accumulates until the sun or a wind change breaks the lid, which is why the worst urban smog episodes and the most stubborn valley fogs are inversion stories, and why a factory chimney's plume on such a morning spreads sideways in a flat ribbon instead of rising.

The same lid explains the mountain surprise in reverse: climb a few hundred meters through the inversion top on a frosty morning and you can walk out of the fog into air several degrees warmer, standing in sunshine above a white sea.
The weather service says it's 20 degrees Fahrenheit with a 25 mph wind, and the 'feels like' is around 3. Is that number made up, or is there a real formula?

There is a real formula — the wind chill index used by North American weather services, fitted from experiments on how fast exposed skin (and water bottles standing in for it) actually loses heat in wind. It is: 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75V^0.16 + 0.4275TV^0.16, with T the air temperature in Fahrenheit and V the wind in miles per hour. Feed in your numbers, T = 20 and V = 25:

About 2.6 °F, which the official chart rounds to 3 — your forecast, audited and confirmed. The formula's limits matter as much as its output: it is defined only for temperatures at or below 50 °F and winds above 3 mph, it assumes exposed skin on a person walking into the wind at night with no sun, and it describes a rate of heat loss, not a temperature anything actually reaches. What it tells you operationally is frostbite time — at a wind chill near zero, exposed skin can freeze in about 30 minutes. Treat 'feels like' as a cooling-rate index wearing a temperature's clothes, and it will never lie to you.

If wind chill makes it 'feel like' 3 degrees when it's really 20, will my car's engine and my garden hose experience 3 degrees too? Will a pipe freeze if the wind chill is below freezing but the air isn't?

No — and this is the most useful correction in all of applied weather. Wind chill is not a temperature that objects fall to; it is a rate at which warm things lose heat. Wind strips away the thin insulating layer of still air that clings to any surface, so a warm object in wind cools toward the air temperature faster. But the air temperature is the floor. Nothing — skin, engine, hose, pipe — can be wind-chilled below the temperature of the air itself, because the wind is only delivering air-temperature air, faster.

So if the air is 20 °F... note the example only bites the other way: if the air is 35 °F with a wind chill of 25 °F, your pipe cannot freeze, full stop — water in it can approach 35 °F and no lower, however hard the wind blows. Gardeners and drivers get real consequences from the rate, though: an engine block reaches ambient temperature in an hour instead of overnight; a warm-blooded animal (including you) must burn fuel continuously to defend its temperature against the accelerated loss, and exposed skin, cooled faster than blood flow can rewarm it, can have its surface driven to the air temperature and frozen — frostbite is your tissue reaching air temperature, not some lower phantom temperature.

The formula belongs to physiology, not plumbing. For pipes, only the thermometer matters — plus how long the cold lasts.
90 degrees Fahrenheit doesn't sound deadly, but with high humidity the heat index hit 106. How does humidity add sixteen degrees?

It doesn't add heat — it subtracts cooling. Your body's only high-power cooling system is evaporation: sweat carries heat away as it turns to vapor. Humid air is already near its vapor capacity, so sweat evaporates slowly or drips uselessly off the skin, and your core temperature climbs toward dangerous levels at air temperatures your body could otherwise handle. The heat index is a regression formula (the Rothfusz fit, used by the US National Weather Service) that maps temperature T and relative humidity R to the temperature that would stress the body equivalently in drier air. For T = 90 °F and R = 70 percent, the full formula gives:

About 106 °F — in the official 'danger' band, where heat exhaustion is likely and heat stroke becomes possible with prolonged exposure. The fine print: the fit assumes shade and light wind; full sun can add the equivalent of up to 15 °F more, and it is calibrated for a typical adult body, not for children, the elderly, or someone working hard. Sixteen phantom degrees is the formula's way of pricing a broken cooling system — and of the two 'feels like' indices, this is the one whose underlying danger (a core temperature your body cannot shed) is the most literal.
Why are cities hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night? I've driven in from rural areas after dark and felt the temperature climb.

You've felt the urban heat island, and its nighttime peak is the key to its mechanism. A city is a different surface than the land it replaced. Asphalt and roofing absorb sunlight efficiently and store it in bulk; concrete and brick are thermal batteries. Vegetation and soil, by contrast, spend much of the sun's energy evaporating water — a cooling expenditure the paved city has largely abolished. Add the waste heat of engines, air conditioners (which move indoor heat outdoors, with interest), furnaces, and industry, plus street canyons that trap radiation between facing walls and block the wind that would carry heat away.

During the day the difference is real but modest — a degree or three Celsius, partly masked because the countryside is also warming. At night the ledger settles: rural ground and vegetation radiate their modest heat quickly and cool deeply, while the city's stored heat leaks out of the pavement for hours, keeping urban air commonly 2–5 °C warmer, and the biggest cities more on still, clear nights. That is why heat waves are deadliest in cities: the night, which is when bodies recover from the day's heat, never actually cools.

The remedies are the mechanisms reversed: trees and vegetation restore evaporation, pale surfaces restore reflection, and spacing restores the wind.
Orchard farmers plant on hillsides instead of the flat valley floor, even though the soil is better in the valley. What do they know about cold air?

They know that on calm, clear nights, cold air behaves like water: it flows downhill and pools. The mechanism is radiation and density. After sunset the ground radiates heat to space and chills the air in contact with it. That chilled air is denser than the air beside it at the same level, so on any slope it begins to slide downhill — slowly, silently, a river of cold a few meters deep — and accumulates in the valley floor and any hollow, deepening through the night. The result is a frost pocket: the valley bottom can sit several degrees colder than the slope a short climb above it, under a temperature inversion of the most local kind.

For a fruit tree, those few degrees at blossom time are the whole crop: blossoms die at temperatures only slightly below freezing, and the valley floor crosses that line on nights the hillside never does. So orchards and vineyards climb the slopes into what growers call the thermal belt — high enough to drain, low enough to farm — and valley floors go to pasture and hay, crops that forgive frost. The same pooling explains why your garden's low corner gets frostbitten first, why fog forms in the hollow before the hill, and why a cold dawn walk uphill can feel like walking into a warmer season.
I learned two different cooling rates for rising air — about 9.8 degrees per kilometer, and about 5.5. Which one is right?

Both — they describe the same air in two different states, and the gap between them is where storms live. The 9.8 °C/km is the dry adiabatic rate: a rising parcel that stays unsaturated cools purely by expansion. Run it up 3 kilometers:

29.4 degrees of cooling. The 5.5 °C/km (it varies, roughly 4–7 depending on temperature) is the saturated rate: once the parcel is condensing cloud, latent heat released by the condensation keeps refunding part of the expansion cooling, so the net cooling is gentler. Up the same 3 kilometers:
Only 16.5 degrees. The difference across that climb:

12.9 degrees — the saturated parcel arrives nearly thirteen degrees warmer than it would have without condensation's refund. That is the thunderstorm's whole business model: a parcel that saturates stays warmer than dry physics would allow, warmer often than the air around it, and so keeps rising. When you hear a forecaster say the atmosphere is 'conditionally unstable,' this is the condition: stable for dry parcels, unstable for saturated ones, with the 12.9-degree refund waiting for whichever parcels get wet.
What's the difference between dew and frost? Some mornings the grass has water droplets, other mornings white crystals, and the temperature seems similar.

The difference is which side of freezing the surface — and the dew point — were on when the deposit formed. Dew is liquid: on a clear calm night a surface radiates heat away, cools to the dew point of the nearby air, and vapor condenses onto it as liquid droplets, exactly as on a cold drink in summer. This happens with the dew point above freezing and the surface settling somewhere above 0 °C as well.

Frost is the same deposition arriving at a colder address. If the surface cools below freezing — and crucially, if the frost point (the saturation temperature with respect to ice) is reached — vapor deposits directly as ice crystals, solid from vapor without a liquid stage, in the feathery patterns that follow the surface's texture. The air temperature on the weather report can read a degree or two above freezing on a frosty morning, because the report is measured in a ventilated shelter a meter and a half up, while the grass radiates itself colder than the air.

A subtle third case: dew that forms as liquid and then freezes when the temperature keeps falling — frozen dew, glassy beads rather than feathery crystals, and the distinction ice-rink black ice on a bridge deck often belongs to this family. Same sky, same night, three deposits — the surface's temperature history decides which.
Deserts are scorching in the day but can be genuinely cold at night. Where does the heat go so fast?

It radiates straight to space, because the desert sky is missing its blanket. Two blankets, actually. The first is water vapor: humid air absorbs much of the infrared radiation the ground emits and re-radiates a good share of it back down, throttling the night's cooling — this is why humid summer nights stay sultry. Desert air holds very little vapor, so the ground's radiation escapes almost unimpeded and the surface temperature plummets after sunset. The second blanket is cloud, also usually absent in deserts for the same dry reasons.

The surface itself conspires: dry sand and rock store heat only in a thin top layer (no water to carry it deeper, and dry soil is a poor conductor), so the day's fierce heat lives in a shallow reservoir that empties quickly once the sun is gone. Temperature swings of 20 °C or more between afternoon and dawn are routine in true deserts — among the largest daily ranges on Earth.

Compare a humid coast at the same latitude: the ocean's enormous heat storage and the vapor-rich air hold the night within a few degrees of the day. The desert's cold night is not an anomaly added to its hot day; both are the same fact — dryness — read at two hours.
What's the actual difference between rain and drizzle? They look like the same thing at different speeds.

Size and birthplace. Drizzle is made of droplets smaller than about half a millimeter — so small and light that they seem to float and drift with every wisp of air. Rain drops are larger, up to several millimeters, and fall decisively. The size difference traces back to the clouds that made them. Drizzle is born in shallow stratus: a thin, gentle cloud with weak updrafts where droplets grow slowly by condensation and modest merging, and never get the long growth journey needed to become rain. It is less a weak rain than a cloud leaking.

True rain usually requires a deeper production line. In cold clouds, the great accelerator is the ice-crystal process: supercooled droplets and ice crystals coexist, vapor preferentially deposits onto the crystals (the air is effectively more supersaturated for ice than for liquid), and crystals grow fast at the droplets' expense until they are heavy enough to fall, melting into raindrops on the way down — most mid-latitude rain, even in summer, began as snow aloft. In warm clouds, rain forms by collision and coalescence: larger droplets fall faster, sweep up smaller ones, and grow by merger. Either way, rain is what precipitation becomes when the cloud gives its droplets room and time to grow up; drizzle is what escapes early.
Why does snow need the whole sky cold, top to bottom? Rain that starts as snow melts, sure, but why can't snow form lower down on its own?

Because snow crystals are born and raised in the cloud, and the cloud's growing zone is a specific cold neighborhood. Snowflakes grow as ice crystals in the part of the cloud roughly between −12 and −16 °C, where the crystal habit — the famous branching dendrite — grows fastest and most elaborately; in warmer cloud layers, crystals grow as stubby plates or columns, and near freezing, growth nearly stalls as liquid water dominates instead. A flake then needs its entire fall to stay below freezing: pass through a layer even a degree or two above 0 °C and it starts melting from the edges; give it a deep warm layer and it arrives as rain.

The atmosphere's temperature profile is thus a gauntlet the flake must run intact. Forecasters obsess over the profile's details because tiny warm layers rewrite the outcome: a thin warm layer aloft partially melts flakes that then refreeze into sleet; a shallow warm layer at the surface with deep cold above it is fine for snow, but the reverse — cold surface, warm nose above — is the freezing-rain trap. 'Will it snow?' is really three questions: will crystals grow well aloft, will the column preserve them, and will the last hundred meters betray them? Snow is the precipitation type with the longest list of ways to fail.
Sleet and freezing rain both start as snow and both involve a warm layer. Why do they end up so different — pellets versus a glaze of ice on everything?

Draw the temperature profile as a layer cake and the difference is one layer's thickness. Both begin the same way: snow falls from a cold cloud into a layer of above-freezing air aloft — the 'warm nose,' typically a shallow wedge of mild air a kilometer or two up. In the warm nose, the flakes melt, fully or mostly. What happens next depends on the cold layer waiting below, near the ground.

If the surface cold layer is deep — hundreds of meters to over a kilometer of subfreezing air — the melted drops have time during their fall to refreeze into solid ice pellets: sleet. You hear it ticking on windows and see it bounce; it accumulates like coarse sand and, while unpleasant, is mechanically manageable.

If the surface cold layer is shallow — a few hundred meters or less — the drops cannot refreeze in time. They arrive at the ground as supercooled liquid: water below 0 °C that has stayed liquid for lack of a trigger. The trigger is contact. The instant a supercooled drop touches a branch, a wire, a road, it freezes on the spot, building a clear, dense glaze. Same storm, same warm nose — the depth of the last cold layer decides whether winter throws pellets or pours glass. It is why two towns thirty kilometers apart in the same storm can report different hazards, and why forecasters speak of the profile with such respect.
Freezing rain terrifies utility companies more than snow does. It's just rain that freezes — why is it so destructive?

Because it doesn't pile up like snow; it accretes, coating everything in clear, dense ice that adds weight exactly where structures can least afford it — on spans. Snow loads roofs from above and much of it slides or sublimates; freezing rain wraps wires, branches, and towers in a growing sleeve of ice. A radial coating of just 12 millimeters on a power line multiplies the line's weight severalfold, and the ice also fattens the line's profile so wind pushes harder on it — the combination of weight and wind load is what brings down poles in sequence, one falling span yanking the next. On trees, the same sleeve can add hundreds of kilograms to a canopy; the cracking you hear in an ice storm is limbs failing under ice they grew themselves.

The physics of the deposit is the supercooling trick: raindrops colder than 0 °C but still liquid freeze on contact, flowing slightly before they set, which is why the glaze is clear and glassy rather than white — it freezes as a coherent sheet, not as crystals with air pockets. Roads get their share too, as a transparent film indistinguishable from wet pavement: black ice in its most literal form.

A snowstorm's damage scales with depth; an ice storm's scales with time, because every hour of freezing rain thickens the sleeve. Half an inch of ice is a bad day. An inch is a regional disaster.
Is graupel just small hail? It looks like tiny styrofoam balls and falls in spring showers.

Cousins, not twins — they are built by different processes and testify about different clouds. Graupel (also called snow pellets) starts life as a snowflake. Falling through a cloud layer rich in supercooled droplets, the flake collects them as rime — the droplets freeze onto its branches on contact, gradually filling in the crystal until it becomes a soft, opaque, crumbly pellet a few millimeters across, like a tiny ball of frost. It is light, fragile, and falls in showery bursts, often from spring cumulus. Squeeze it and it crushes.

Hail starts as an ice embryo in a thunderstorm and grows by sweeping up supercooled water in powerful updrafts, building dense, hard, often layered ice — a stone, not a pellet. It is a product of violent vertical motion and can reach sizes graupel never approaches.

The distinction is diagnostic. Graupel tells you: convective showers with supercooled droplets and modest updrafts — a chilly, unstable day. Hail tells you: a thunderstorm with updrafts strong enough to suspend growing ice, possibly repeatedly. Both are 'ice pellets' to a casual glance, but one is rimed snow and the other is a thunderstorm's ammunition, and a forecaster reads them as differently as a doctor reads a cough versus a fever.
The Sahara, the Arabian desert, the Australian outback — they all sit at roughly the same latitudes. That can't be a coincidence. What parks deserts there?

It is not a coincidence; it is the exhaust of the tropics. Follow the great circulation: at the equator, intense sun drives air upward in towering thunderstorms (the rising branch of the Hadley cell). That air travels poleward at high altitude, cools, and — around 25 to 30 degrees of latitude, north and south — descends back toward the surface in a broad belt around the planet. Descending air is the desert-maker, by the same physics as a high-pressure system: as it sinks it is compressed and warms, its relative humidity collapses, clouds dissolve in it, and rain becomes nearly impossible. Under this subtropical high belt, the air at the surface is perpetually air that has been wrung out and dried by descent. That is the Sahara's address, and Arabia's, and the Australian interior's, and the Kalahari's, and the Atacama and Sonoran's in the other hemisphere and the Americas.

The belt explains the map's big pattern, and local effects paint the details: cold ocean currents stabilize the air along some coasts and deepen the aridity (the Atacama and Namib are the driest places on Earth partly for this reason), and mountain rain shadows carve additional dry pockets at other latitudes. But the latitude clustering you noticed is the fingerprint of a planetary machine: deserts live where the sky's air comes down.
The forecast says 25 centimeters of snow. A friend says that's 'only' 25 millimeters of water. Is the ten-to-one thing real?
The ten-to-one ratio is the standard first approximation, and your friend's arithmetic follows it:

25 centimeters of snow at a 10:1 ratio melts down to 2.5 centimeters — 25 millimeters — of water. The ratio is the snowpack's density in disguise: fresh snow at 10:1 is about a tenth as dense as water. But the ratio is a variable wearing a constant's clothes. Cold, dry, fluffy snow falling in very cold air can run 15:1, 20:1, even fluffier; wet spring snow, falling near freezing with liquid water in it, can be 5:1:

The same 25 centimeters then carries 5 centimeters of water — twice the weight on roofs, twice the meltwater in rivers, and a completely different shoveling experience. Forecasters who take snow seriously forecast the water content and the ratio separately, using the temperature profile of the storm. Ten-to-one is a fair guess for an average storm and a poor one for any particular storm — which is why your friend's 'only' deserves a raised eyebrow in March and a nod in January.
Sometimes I see rain streaks falling from clouds that never reach the ground — they just fade out halfway down. And I read those can cause sudden dangerous winds. How?

The fading streaks are virga: precipitation falling from a cloud into a layer of dry air and evaporating on the way down. Each droplet shrinks as it falls through the unsaturated layer; small drops may vanish entirely kilometers above the ground. The cloud is raining; the earth just never receives the delivery.

The danger is in what evaporation does to that dry layer. Evaporation is a cooling process — the same 2.5 million joules per kilogram, now extracted from the air the rain falls through. The cooled air becomes denser and starts to sink, and as it sinks it can accelerate, dragging more rain into itself and evaporating more — a self-reinforcing downdraft. When that column of cold air hits the ground it splashes outward violently: a dry microburst, a sudden blast of wind that arrives under a sky where no rain ever lands. Aircraft on approach have been caught by exactly this — a strong downdraft and outflow beneath an innocent-looking cloud with pretty veils under it.

So virga is not failed weather; it is weather whose energy got spent in the air instead of delivered to the ground. The streaks' graceful fade is the visible signature of evaporation doing mechanical work.
Fifty millimeters of rain fell on our house's roof in one storm. How much water is that, actually? The roof is about 100 square meters.
Fifty millimeters is a depth — 0.05 meters of water standing on every surface. Spread over your 100 square meters of roof:
5 cubic meters of water intercepted by the roof alone. In the units a water tank would use:

5,000 liters — five tonnes of water, delivered from the sky in a few hours, which your gutters were asked to collect and your downpipes to drain. This is why roof area, not garden area, is the number rainwater-harvesting people care about: even modest rain on a modest roof is tonnes. It is also the arithmetic behind urban flooding: pave a neighborhood and every roof and road becomes a collector like yours, concentrating the storm's water into drains at a speed the old soil never imposed. The storm drops the same 50 millimeters either way; the landscape decides whether it arrives as a soak or a surge.
Cities downwind of the Great Lakes get buried in snow while places fifty kilometers inland get flurries. The lakes aren't that big. What amplifies the snow so much?

Lake-effect snow is a moisture-harvesting machine with a simple design and extravagant output. The setup: very cold, dry arctic air — often 10 to 20 degrees colder than the lake surface — streams across a long fetch of open, relatively warm water. The lake evaporates vigorously into the frigid air (you can see it as steam fog over the water), and the heated, moistened bottom layer becomes unstable: it starts convecting in narrow bands of cloud streets aligned with the wind. In the space of a lake crossing, bone-dry polar air loads itself with water vapor it never had.

Then the shoreline ends the free ride. The air hits land, friction slows the surface flow, the air piles up and is forced to rise — and rising saturated air with a grudge dumps its harvested moisture as intense snow bands, sometimes at rates of 5 centimeters an hour or more, in corridors only a few kilometers wide. Step outside the band and the sun may be shining; drive five kilometers sideways and you are in a whiteout. That narrowness is why the contrasts are so violent over short distances.

The machine's requirements explain its geography and season: it needs the lake unfrozen (ice caps the evaporation), a long fetch (wind aligned with the lake's long axis), and the big air-water temperature contrast of late autumn and early winter, before the lakes chill or freeze. It is the sea-breeze principle's winter sibling: a water body spending its stored warmth into cold air, and the downwind shore collecting the payment as snow.
When forecasters show those 'spaghetti plots' with twenty lines going in different directions, is that twenty different opinions? What am I looking at?

You are looking at one forecaster's honest uncertainty, drawn. An ensemble is a set of model runs — often 20 to 50 — of the same weather model (or a family of them) started from slightly different initial conditions, each perturbed within the range of what the observations could really be saying, since no observation network measures the whole atmosphere exactly. Each line is one run's answer: a hurricane's track, a temperature curve, a front's position.

Where the lines bundle tightly together for days, the atmosphere is in a mood that doesn't care about small errors — the forecast is robust, and you can trust it more than usual. Where the lines fan out into spaghetti, small differences are amplifying: the atmosphere is near a fork, and the honest forecast is a probability distribution, not a path. Professionals read the fan-out point as the practical horizon of confidence for that situation.

The ensemble's average is usually more accurate than any single 'best' run, and its spread is information no single run can give you: it is the difference between 'rain on Thursday' and 'rain on Thursday, give or take two days, and here's how the alternatives look.' Spaghetti is not indecision. It is the forecast showing its work.
Why are forecasts decent for three days out, shaky at seven, and basically fiction at fourteen? What's the wall they hit?

The wall is chaos — in the technical sense: the atmosphere amplifies small errors, relentlessly. A weather model starts from observations that are incomplete and slightly wrong: no instrument measures every cubic meter, so the model's initial state differs from the real atmosphere by small amounts everywhere. Those small differences don't stay small. In a fluid full of interacting eddies and storms, errors roughly double on a timescale of a couple of days, fed by every scale of motion down to individual thunderstorms the model can't even resolve. A hairline misjudgment of today's wind field becomes a misplaced shower in two days, a misplaced front in four, a wrong air mass in a week.

Better models, denser observations, and faster computers have pushed the wall back — today's five-day forecast is about as skillful as the three-day forecast of a few decades ago — but they push against mathematics, not just engineering. Beyond roughly two weeks, the doubled errors have grown to the size of the weather itself, and a deterministic forecast contains no more information than climatology: what usually happens in that season.

This is also why honest forecasters talk in probabilities and ensembles at long range. The wall isn't a failure of effort; it is a property of the atmosphere's equations, discovered by running the same model twice with nearly identical starts and watching the two futures divorce.
The forecast says '30% chance of rain.' Thirty percent of what — the day? The area? My plans always hinge on this.

It is a probability about a point, and the formal definition is worth knowing exactly. The probability of precipitation (PoP) is the likelihood that a measurable amount — at least 0.01 inches — falls at any given point in the forecast area during the period. Formally, forecasters construct it as confidence times area: PoP = C × A, where C is the forecaster's confidence that rain will occur somewhere in the area, and A is the fraction of the area expected to receive it. If a forecaster is 100% certain that 30% of the county will get measurable rain, the PoP for your point is 30% — because your chance of being in the rained-on third is 30%. If rain is certain to cover half the area, PoP is 50%; if a system is a coin flip but would cover everything if it comes, PoP is also 50%.

What it is not: not 30% of the day raining, not 30% of the rain you'd get in a storm, and not '30% of forecasters agree.' For your plans, the translation is: over many days with a 30% forecast at your location, it rains on about three of them. A 30% day is a 'bring the umbrella if the stakes are high' day, not a 'cancel the picnic' day. And a 90% day with a cold front is a different animal from a 90% day of scattered sea-breeze showers — the number is a point probability, and the accompanying text tells you which kind of rain is gambling against you.
A forecaster said she was '80% confident rain would cover half the county,' and the app showed 40% chance of rain. Did the app just make up a number?
No — the app multiplied exactly what she said. The probability of precipitation at any given point is confidence times coverage:

0.4 — a 40% chance that any particular point (your garden) receives measurable rain. The logic is a two-step lottery: first the system must materialize (80% confidence), then your point must lie in the covered half (50%), and the joint probability is the product. Ensembles give forecasters a second way to land on the same kind of number. If 14 of 20 ensemble runs produce rain at your point:

70% — the fraction of simulated futures in which you get wet, which is often how the app's number was actually built. Either way, the percentage is not a measure of how hard it will rain or for how long; it is strictly the odds of at least a measurable amount. Two days can both read 40% and be utterly different: one a likely brief shower, the other a 40% chance of a washout. The number is honest; it just answers a narrower question than the one picnics ask.
Weather radar shows green, yellow, and red blobs. Is red just 'heavy rain'? What is the radar actually measuring?

Radar measures echoes, not rain. The radar sends out pulses of microwave energy and listens for what bounces back from raindrops, snowflakes, hail, insects, and occasionally the atmosphere itself. The strength of the returned signal — reflectivity, reported in dBZ — grows with both the number of particles and, steeply, their size: reflectivity scales with the sixth power of droplet diameter, so a few large drops outshout a swarm of small ones. The colors are reflectivity bands: greens are typically light precipitation, yellows moderate, reds heavy — or something that merely looks heavy to the radar.

That last caveat is where honesty enters. Converting reflectivity to a rainfall rate requires assuming a drop-size distribution (the Z–R relationship), and nature doesn't always comply: hail produces screaming red echoes while contributing no rain at all until it melts; a 'bright band' appears where snow melts into rain, the wet flakes mimicking huge drops; tropical drizzle can pour respectably from unimpressive greens because its drops are numerous but small. Modern dual-polarization radars interrogate particle shape as well and have narrowed these ambiguities a lot, letting forecasters distinguish rain from hail from — famously — tornado debris.

So the map is a measurement with a model folded inside it. Red means 'strong echo,' heavy rain is its usual but not its only author, and the forecaster's job includes knowing which author is writing today.
What's the difference between a 'nowcast' and a forecast? My app updates the next-hour rain prediction constantly.

Timescale and method. A forecast, in the strict sense, comes from a numerical weather prediction model: physics equations run forward on a supercomputer from an analyzed starting state, producing the next hours to days. It knows about fronts that haven't arrived and storms that haven't formed — it can predict weather that doesn't exist yet, which is its glory and its error source.

A nowcast covers roughly the next zero to six hours and leans on what is actually happening now: the radar's current echoes, satellite motion, surface observations, extrapolated forward and corrected minute by minute. Your app's next-hour rain call is mostly nowcasting — it sees the shower on radar, tracks its motion and trend, and tells you the rain starts in 18 minutes. Within its short window, a nowcast typically beats the big model, because it starts from reality rather than from a simulation of reality.

The trade is reach. Extrapolation cannot foresee development: it cannot predict the storm that will form at 4 p.m. from a clear 1 p.m. sky, or the existing storm's sudden death. So the craft is blended in practice: nowcast logic dominates the first hours, model physics takes over beyond, and the app quietly hands off between them. When the next-hour prediction is eerily precise, thank observation; when the weekend outlook is good, thank the model; when either is wrong, you now know which tool to blame.
The forecast for the airport said clear, but my valley had fog until ten. Was the forecast wrong, or just not about my valley?

Probably the second — and the distinction matters for how much you should trust forecasts generally. A forecast is verified at observation points, and the official observation for your region is likely the airport: a flat, paved, wind-exposed site chosen for aviation, not a hollow where cold air pools. Your valley runs its own microclimate. On a clear calm night, radiational cooling chills the slopes, cold dense air drains down and ponds in your bottom land, and the pond saturates into fog — while the airport, a few meters higher or better ventilated, never reaches saturation. Both observations are true; they are about different air.

Forecasts are issued for areas, and within any area the terrain writes footnotes: frost pockets and fog hollows, ridge tops that catch wind the valley escapes, the south-facing slope that thaws at noon, the lakeshore strip that runs five degrees milder. A good local forecast names these when they matter ('patchy fog in low-lying areas'), but no area forecast can carry every hollow's private weather.

The mature way to use a forecast is as the regional script, with your own knowledge of your ground as the local amendment. After a season of watching, residents of fog hollows learn their offset from the airport's story — how many extra hours their fog lasts, how much colder their dawns run. That calibration is real meteorological knowledge, earned the slow way.
I keep reading that forecast errors 'double every couple of days.' If a model starts with a small error, how fast does it actually blow up?

Take the doubling time as about two and a half days — a fair mid-range figure for the growth of small errors in modern models — and start with an error of 1 unit, say a 1-degree temperature misjudgment somewhere in the initial data. After five days, two doublings:
The error has grown to 4 units. After seven and a half days, three doublings:

8 units. Keep the arithmetic running and by two weeks the initial 1-degree blemish has multiplied by a factor of about fifty — the size of the weather signal itself, at which point the forecast and reality are strangers. This is the quantitative skeleton under the rule that forecasts decay: skill doesn't fade linearly, it is eroded by an exponential working against a fixed-size signal, which is why the practical horizon sits near two weeks no matter how good the model gets. Improvements in observations and computing buy real days — the doubling time stretches, the initial error shrinks — but the exponential always collects its debt. Every long-range forecast is a loan against that arithmetic.
If weather models are so powerful, why can't they just tell me if it will rain on my street at 4 p.m. next Tuesday?

Because your street is smaller than the model's eyes. A global forecast model divides the atmosphere into grid boxes — the best operational ones are around 10 kilometers on a side, with the state of the whole box summarized by single values at each level. Your street shares its box with a whole suburb, a hill, and part of a lake. Worse, the most important rain-makers are smaller than any grid box: a thunderstorm cell is a few kilometers wide, and the cloud droplets inside it are micrometers. Clouds and convection therefore cannot be simulated directly; they are parameterized — represented by statistical recipes that say, in effect, 'when a box is this warm and this moist, this fraction of it probably convects.' The recipes are good, but they are educated summaries, not physics at full resolution.

Regional models zoom in to boxes of 1–4 kilometers and can begin to grow explicit storms, which is why short-range local forecasts have improved so much — but only for a day or two ahead, and only over limited areas, because computation is finite.

So 'rain on your street at 4 p.m. Tuesday' asks for three precisions the system cannot jointly offer: street-scale space, hour-scale time, week-scale range. What it can honestly say is the probability that your grid box sees rain in that window, and the likely character of it. The forecast isn't being coy; its resolution is a physical fact about the tool, like a microscope's.
When a forecaster says '70% chance of rain,' how would anyone ever check whether they're any good? One day either rains or it doesn't.

By keeping score over hundreds of days — probability forecasts are graded as a population, not as single calls. The key property is reliability: gather every day the forecaster said 70%, and check what fraction of those days actually delivered rain at your point. If it is close to 70%, the probabilities are honest — calibrated. If it rained on only 40% of their '70%' days, they are systematically overconfident, however scientific their models. The mirror-image failure is the forecaster who always says 30% in a climate where it rains 30% of days: perfectly calibrated, and perfectly useless, because the forecast never distinguishes one day from another. Skill needs both calibration and sharpness — the willingness to say 5% and 95% when the evidence warrants, and to be right at the stated rates.

Formal scores (the Brier score is the classic) combine these into one number that punishes both overconfidence and hedging. This is also why weather services publish verification statistics and why the modern probability era is a genuine advance over the old categorical one. '70%' is not a fudge to avoid being wrong; it is a claim precise enough to be audited — and the audit, over a season, is ruthless. A forecaster whose 70s verify at 70 has earned the right to be believed at 90.
Old weather lore says a ring around the moon means rain soon. Is there anything to it, or is it pure superstition?

There is a mechanism under this one, which is why it survived. The ring — a halo at a fixed radius around the sun or moon — is made by moonlight refracting through ice crystals in cirrostratus cloud, a high, thin, uniform veil. Cirrostratus is significant not for itself but for what it usually belongs to: the advancing cloud shield of a warm front, where the cloud sequence runs cirrus, then cirrostratus, then lower and thicker sheets, then rain. The halo is an early chapter of that sequence — the front's moisture arriving at high altitude a day or so ahead of its surface position. In the mid-latitudes, where traveling frontal systems are the main rain-makers, a halo genuinely is followed by rain within roughly 12 to 24 hours often enough to have built its reputation honestly.

The limits are the usual ones for lore. Cirrostratus can occur without a front — in the debris of distant storms, in jet-stream moisture — and then the halo promises nothing. And the lore is regional: it encodes the mid-latitude west-to-east procession of systems, and exports poorly to the tropics or to climates where rain comes from afternoon convection instead. The rhyme is a compressed climatology: true where it was written, for the reasons it implies, and silent about everywhere else. That is more than can be said for most superstitions.
Airplane contrails sometimes vanish in seconds and sometimes spread out and cover the sky. Can they really tell me something about the air up there?

They can — a contrail is a free probe of the upper atmosphere's humidity, flown for you at 10 kilometers. A jet exhaust adds water vapor and particles to very cold air; the vapor condenses and freezes into a line of ice crystals. What happens next is entirely about the air the trail is deposited in. If the ambient air at that level is dry — well below ice saturation — the crystals evaporate quickly and the trail dies within seconds to minutes. If the air is near or above ice saturation, the crystals cannot evaporate; they persist, grow by taking up the air's excess vapor, and spread under wind shear into broad cirrus-like sheets that can last for hours.

So the sky writes its own report: short-lived trails, dry air aloft; long-lived, spreading trails, a moist layer overhead — and moisture arriving aloft is one of the ingredients in pattern changes, often preceding an approaching frontal system by a day or so, since fronts export their moisture at high levels first. Pilots and forecasters both read them this way. One boundary to keep: contrails are made of exactly what cirrus is made of — ice — and behave under the same physics. They are artificial clouds, and like natural ones, their lifetime is the humidity of their neighborhood made visible.
'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning.' I know it's a rhyme, but is there actual physics in it?

There is — enough that the rhyme exists in many cultures and even made it into ancient texts. The color first: at sunrise and sunset, sunlight crosses a long slant of atmosphere, and the blue end of the spectrum is scattered away en route, leaving the reds to illuminate whatever clouds are present. The question is which clouds, and where.

In the mid-latitudes, weather systems travel predominantly west to east. At sunset, the sun is in the west — the direction your weather is coming from. A red sunset means the low western sun is shining through clear, dry air (only clear air lets the reddened light travel that far unobstructed) and lighting the clouds overhead or to the east — the departing system. Clear air to the west is tomorrow's air arriving: delight, fairly earned. At sunrise the geometry reverses: red light means clear air to the east — yesterday's fair weather leaving — while the sun illuminates cloud to the west, the incoming direction: the next system is already on stage. Warning, fairly earned.

The rhyme's fine print is its birthplace. It assumes the mid-latitude westerlies; in the tropics, where weather rides the easterlies, the logic inverts or dissolves, and anywhere, a red sky caused by dust or smoke rather than cloud breaks the code entirely. It is a local instrument, accurate at home: a one-line summary of storm-track climatology plus optics.
Pilots seem to pay a lot of attention to those smooth lens-shaped clouds over mountains. Besides looking strange, what do they tell a pilot?

A lenticular is a signed certificate that a mountain wave is running — and the wave system that draws such a pretty signature aloft often includes a violent basement. The lens sits at a wave crest, where air rises and condenses; but the same standing wave, near the ground on the lee side, frequently organizes a rotor: a tumbling, horizontal-axis circulation under the crest where the airflow is chaotic and turbulent in a way that has damaged aircraft. The smooth cloud marks the smooth part of the wave; the danger is the invisible part beneath it. Pilots also read lenticulars as a direct wind gauge: the wave only forms when winds aloft are strong and increasing with height, blowing fairly perpendicular to the ridge — so a stack of lenses (sometimes several, at different levels, like a pile of plates) reports strong upper flow and a stable layer structure without a single instrument.

Sailplane pilots exploit the same system deliberately, climbing in the wave's rising branches to extraordinary altitudes — the wave that endangers the careless is a free elevator to those who read it. For the rest of us, the lens over the ridge is a forecast in one image: strong winds aloft, turbulence near the terrain, and — because wave clouds need a stable layer — often fair weather at the surface despite the drama overhead.
Is 'the calm before the storm' real, or do people just remember the quiet because the storm was loud?

Mostly memory doing editing — but with a real phenomenon buried in it, which is why the saying refuses to die. Start with the audit: people notice a lull before a dramatic storm because contrast makes it memorable; the many storms that arrive without any lull, and the many lulls followed by nothing, leave no story. As a rule for prediction, 'it feels eerily calm' is unreliable, and forecasters do not use it.

The buried truth is that certain storms do manufacture a local calm by their geometry. Ahead of an organized storm line, the low-level flow feeding the storm can temporarily overpower the ambient wind, producing a still, oppressive interval — the inflow gathering itself. Separately, the most famous calm in meteorology is real but misplaced in the saying: the eye of a hurricane is a genuine, profound calm, but it is the middle of the storm, not the herald. And there is a third honest case: on a hot unstable afternoon, the whole boundary layer can go briefly quiet as cumulus congestus towers overhead shade the ground and kill the thermals that were stirring the air — a hush that really does precede the first downdraft by minutes.

So: the phenomenon exists in pieces, each with a mechanism, none dependable. The saying survives because memory keeps the hits. A good sky-watcher files it under 'sometimes, and here's why,' which is where most weather lore belongs after an audit.
I timed the thunder from two lightning flashes ten minutes apart: 15 seconds, then 6 seconds. Can I work out how fast the storm is approaching?
You have everything you need — sound travels about 343 meters per second, so each count is a distance. First flash, 15 seconds:
The storm was 5,145 meters away. Second flash, ten minutes later, 6 seconds:
2,058 meters. The distance it closed in those 600 seconds:
3,087 meters. Divide by the elapsed time for the approach speed:

About 5.1 meters per second — roughly 18–19 kilometers per hour, a typical pace for a thunderstorm cell being steered by the mid-level winds. At that rate it covers the remaining two kilometers in about six to seven minutes, which is the practical output of your arithmetic: head inside now. Two honest caveats: you timed two different bolts, possibly from different parts of a sprawling storm, so treat the speed as an estimate of the storm's near edge, not a train schedule; and lightning can strike from the storm's anvil well ahead of its rain — distance to the thunder is not a guaranteed safe margin.
In the morning there are little puffy clouds. Some days they stay small and harmless; other days they grow into towers by noon. Can I tell which kind of day it is from the clouds themselves?

Yes — the morning cumulus are reporting the atmosphere's stability in real time, and the difference is visible in their shape and edges. On a stable day, the puffs are flat-topped and modest: each thermal rises, condenses, then hits air warm enough aloft to stop it, and the cloud spreads a little and dies. The clouds look soft, fibrous at the edges, and they shrink as fast as they form — the sky is rationing vertical growth, and afternoon will look much like morning.

On an unstable day the same puffs behave like they have somewhere to be. They grow taller than they are wide, with hard, cauliflower edges and bright, crisp tops — signs of vigorous condensation in a strong updraft that is still accelerating. Individual towers merge, darken at the base as they deepen, and by early afternoon the tallest may sprout the fibrous, icy anvil texture at their tops. The morning tell is the vertical ambition: cumulus that are visibly building upward through the late morning, in an air mass with high dew points, are the atmosphere announcing that parcels are reaching their free-convection level unaided.

Glider pilots have made this read for a century: flat and fraying means a capped day, tall and hard-edged means climb rates and possibly storms. Your eyes, plus the rule 'height beats width means trouble,' will sort most days correctly.
Before a thunderstorm arrives I sometimes feel a sudden cool wind from the wrong direction, and the temperature drops in a minute. The rain hasn't started. What is that?

That is the storm's exhaust arriving ahead of it: the gust front. Inside a mature thunderstorm, rain falling into dry air evaporates and chills the air it passes through, and that dense, rain-cooled air sinks in the downdraft and then spreads outward along the ground like water poured from a bucket — a shallow river of cold air, sometimes only a few hundred meters deep, racing away from the storm in all directions, fastest in the direction the storm is moving. Its leading edge is the gust front.

When it passes you, every element of your observation checks out: the wind shifts suddenly because the flow is now the storm's outflow, not the day's ambient wind; it comes 'from the wrong direction' because it radiates from the storm, not from the prevailing flow; the temperature drops several degrees in a minute because the air is literally the storm's refrigerated exhaust; and it arrives before the rain because the outflow outruns the storm cell itself, sometimes by 10–20 kilometers. Dust lines, a sudden stirring of trees in sequence across a field, and a dark shelf cloud marking the front's position in the sky are its visible signatures.

The gust front is also a storm-maker in its own right: its leading edge lifts the warm moist air ahead of it, and new cells often ignite along it — which is how one storm gives birth to the next, and how storm lines sustain themselves for hours.
At 6 p.m. it's 8 degrees and the dew point is 7. The evening is cooling at about 1.5 degrees an hour. Can I predict dew — or frost — tonight?
You can predict the timing of the dew, at least. The temperature needs to fall to the dew point — a gap of one degree at your cooling rate:

About 40 minutes — so by roughly 6:40 p.m., surfaces that cool at the air's rate reach saturation and dew begins; exposed surfaces like grass and car roofs, which radiate faster than the air cools, will get there sooner. Whether it becomes frost is a second question: frost requires the surface to reach the frost point at or below 0 °C, and with a dew point of 7 °C there is a long way to fall — on these numbers, dew is certain and frost is out of reach unless the night turns far colder than the current trend. The general instrument you've just used is the evening spread: temperature minus dew point, small and closing, means dew or fog; a dew point below freezing with clear calm skies means frost is the deposit to expect. Gardeners who check two numbers at suppertime — the spread and the dew point against zero — can call most nights correctly.
After rain, the wet earth has that wonderful smell — and sometimes I smell it before the rain even arrives. What is that smell, physically?

Most of it is biology's perfume: geosmin, a compound produced by soil bacteria (actinomycetes) as they grow and form spores in dry earth. Human noses are absurdly sensitive to geosmin — we detect it at a few parts per trillion, a sensitivity that rivals a shark's for blood and presumably once paid for itself by pointing our ancestors at water and workable soil. When rain strikes dry ground, the impact launches tiny aerosol droplets that carry geosmin and plant oils — the full mixture is called petrichor — into the air you breathe.

The smelling-it-beforehand is real too, and it is the storm announcing itself chemically. A thunderstorm's downdraft is air that has traveled from high in the storm, and it can carry ozone — created by lightning's electrical discharge splitting oxygen molecules aloft — down to the surface and outward ahead of the rain. Ozone has a sharp, clean, almost chlorine-like tang, and it rides the gust front, arriving minutes before the rain does. Some of the pre-rain smell is also petrichor from the storm's own first rain falling on dry ground upwind, delivered to you by that same outflow.

So your nose is running a two-channel forecast: the sweet earthy note says rain is falling on dry soil somewhere near; the sharp electric note says a storm's downdraft is already on its way. Both channels are mechanism, not magic.
